newsitem.title: DUBAI: Visits boost nurses' morale in Saudi murder case.
newsitem.headline: Visits boost nurses' morale in Saudi murder case.

text.p: The families of two British nurses charged with murder in Saudi Arabia visited them in jail on Sunday for the second day in a row, boosting their spirits and morale, the women's lawyer said.

Deborah Parry, 41, and Lucille McLauchlan, 31 -- charged with killing Australian colleague Yvonne Gilford in December -- saw their relatives at the Dammam central prison in eastern Saudi Arabia, Salah al-Hejailan told Reuters.

Parry and McLauchlan have pleaded not guilty to murdering their 55-year-old colleague in her room at the King Fahd military medical complex in December. Medical reports said Gilford had been stabbed 13 times, bludgeoned and suffocated.
"The visits were very good for the morale of the girls. They are more determined than ever before to defend themselves. The visits enhanced their determination and their attitude."
Hejailan said Parry had met with her sister Sandra and her brother-in-law Jonathan Ashbee, while McLauchlan met with her father Stan and her fiance Grant Ferrie.
"They will see the nurses again on Monday and may return to Britain on Tuesday," he said.
Parry and McLauchlan said in an open letter to Yvonne's brother Frank Gilford, released on Saturday, that their confessions to Saudi investigators were made under duress.
"We are mentally and physically incapable of inflicting the vicious and extensive injuries which Yvonne suffered," the women said in the letter, a signed copy of which was sent to Reuters.

"In the process of extracting these confessions, we were subjected to sexual threats and interrogation tactics that confused and frightened us especially after long hours without sleep and while suffering severe anxiety," the letter said.
The women also denied allegations of a lesbian relationship with Gilford, whom they described as a friend.

A Saudi court adjourned a hearing in the case for three weeks on May 25 to allow Gilford's family time to consider a settlement which could spare the lives of the accused. The trial is set to resume on June 15, the lawyers said.

Islamic sharia law enforced in Saudi Arabia allows the victim's family to decide for or against execution, which in Saudi Arabia is traditionally carried out by public beheading. Gilford's brother Frank has said he favours the death penalty.
"Yvonne was stabbed in the chest and neck and abdomen and back," said Jim Phipps, a lawyer at the International Law Firm in Riyadh which represents the victim's family.

"The basis for the Gilfords' decision in this matter is in large part related to the way that Yvonne was killed," said Phipps, adding that Frank Gilford was not planning to come to Saudi Arabia for the trial.
The nurses have urged Gilford to reconsider his decision.

"Please understand that we are not seeking your forgiveness, but we are seeking your cooperation in the way which the judges have requested," the women said in their letter. "We appeal to you to listen to our story and we are sure you will then be convinced of our innocence."
